result:
There is a strange fact I keep turning over: we have better maps of the surface of Mars than of the floor of our own oceans. Mars has been photographed in fine detail by orbiters for decades, and the Moon has been mapped down to craters a few meters wide. The seafloor, which covers most of the planet and sits directly beneath the ships that cross it, remains mostly a blur. Estimates vary, but only about a quarter of it has been charted at high resolution. The rest is guesswork, interpolated from satellite measurements of gravity and a scattering of soundings taken by ships that were going somewhere else.

I find this thrilling in a way I can't fully justify. It means that somewhere below the surface of a sea I could drive to in an afternoon, there are mountain ranges I have never seen, canyons deeper than the Grand Canyon is wide, and volcanoes that nobody has photographed. Some of them probably have names now, given by the people who first mapped them, and most of those names are plain and practical. Ridges get named after research vessels. Seamounts get named after the ships that found them, or after whoever signed the paperwork. Once in a while someone gets poetic and names a feature after a myth or a lost sailor, and those names feel like small lights in the dark.

The sonar itself is a kind of miracle of patience. A ship sends sound pulses downward and listens for the echoes. The time it takes for the echo to return gives the depth, and a long line of these measurements, stitched together, gives a profile of the bottom. It is slow work. A ship mapping a patch of seafloor moves back and forth in tight lines, like someone mowing a lawn in the dark, and the resulting image is built one ping at a time. Nothing about it is instant. You cannot look down and see the bottom the way you look at a hill. You have to trust the arithmetic and wait.

I suspect that is part of why the subject moves me. Most of what matters in a life is unseen in exactly this way. A friendship that has run quietly for thirty years is mapped mostly by its echoes: a letter, a phone call, a sentence that lands precisely because the other person remembers something you said long ago. A person's character is less a visible surface than a bathymetry, the shape of what they have carried and where they have been pushed. We glimpse the peaks, the moments of obvious drama, and we infer the rest, and we are often wrong about the rest in ways we only discover when the sonar finally passes over a part we had assumed was flat.

There is also something humbling about the pressure down there. At the deepest points of the ocean, the water above weighs enough to crush most of the equipment we send. Creatures that live there have adapted to a world without sunlight, where the food arrives as slow drifts of dead matter from the surface, and where some animals produce their own light to find each other. I like to imagine that these animals have their own unmapped lives, their own rivalries and courtships and routines, going on with no witnesses at all. The fact that they are not observed does not make them less real. It only makes them private.

I think we are drawn to maps partly because they promise that nothing will be lost. A map says: this is here, and you can go back to it. But the seafloor reminds me that the most important territories often resist that promise. You can measure them, you can name them, and still they stay largely dark. Perhaps this is fine. Perhaps some parts of the world are meant to remain approximate, so that we keep a sense of wonder about what we have not yet touched.

I am not sure what I would do with a perfect map of the ocean floor, if one existed tomorrow. I suspect I would spend hours tracing the ridges with a fingertip, and then I would close the file and feel slightly disappointed, the way you feel when a mystery is solved and the solution is ordinary. The mystery was the good part. The not-knowing was a kind of room to think in.

So I find myself hoping the mapping goes slowly. I hope the ships keep sweeping back and forth, the pings keep returning, and the blurry parts gradually sharpen without ever quite finishing. There is something comforting about a world that still has depths we have not sounded, and about the idea that for every confident line on a chart, there is a dark valley somewhere that has not yet been named, going about its business under a great weight of water, waiting for someone to listen for the echo.
